summary:
Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), and the law reaches far beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) documents that the SSMPA also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case surfaced in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
The Thomson Reuters Foundation's August 2024 assessment, marking ten years of the SSMPA, finds that the law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its statutory scope and has effectively sanctioned abuse; LGBTQ+ Nigerians report lost job prospects and a rise in attacks since its passage.

Community infrastructure exists because state protection does not. Queer Nigerians counter app-based entrapment with exposure forums and sting operations; one administrator's alert page drawing 43,000 followers is cited as the scale of that self-policing.

Two official foreign assessments point in the same direction across a decade: the UK Home Office's 2025-2026 country policy note sets out penalties as they stand in law, while the UK foreign office's 2026 travel advice sets out the consequences for visitors, including attacks, blackmail and death-penalty exposure. The gap between the statute's text and its enforcement practice is itself a safety variable: police extortion is reported against people stopped for appearance rather than conduct.

Where trans identity is not named in the criminal statute, discretion fills the gap. The prison-placement question raised in the Bobrisky case shows that transgender detainees face unregulated outcomes under general correctional rules, and the cross-dressing proposals reported by Reuters show that expression, not identity, is the legislative target.
localsOnly:
Nigerian LGBTQ+ residents face the consequences of a decade of enforcement documented in the Thomson Reuters Foundation's 2024 review: lost employment, rising attacks, and extortion by police who invoke the SSMPA regardless of whether the conduct falls within it.

Residents of the twelve northern states operate under two criminal regimes at once, since Sharia law in those states criminalises same-sex acts between women as well as men and prescribes the death penalty for male sodomy, layered on the federal statute.

Internal accountability exists in narrow form. The October 2024 investigative panel into the Bobrisky case dismissed bribery allegations but ruled that placing her in a maximum-security prison breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, since she was a first-time offender; the finding concerns prison administration rather than protection of trans detainees.

Residents also carry the domestic policing burden that visitors share: arbitrary stops, violence and payoffs, as reported in the Lagos case of Okafor and catalogued by Human Rights Watch since 2016.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the cross-dressing criminalisation proposals reported by Reuters in September 2022 have since been enacted. The available sources describe them as proposals and do not record a final legislative outcome.

Unresolved: whether Bobrisky was assigned to a male or a female prison section during her 2024 term. The source available does not record the decision, only that the choice was reported as discretionary at the time of sentencing.

Unresolved: the current status of the investigation into the killing of Abuja Area Mama. The sources record that no suspects had been charged six months after the August 2024 killing, despite an announced investigation by the Abuja police chief; no later outcome is sourced here.

Not sourced in this inventory: whether Nigeria's entry or visa screening involves any question about gender identity or transition history, or whether foreign consular officials require documents that match gender presentation at the border. Any claim on border screening would need a dedicated source.
